title: Broomfield County Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Broomfield County wells have a 35 ft median recorded depth, but monitoring wells dominate the records. Compare yields, costs and buying risks.
h1: What Broomfield County Well Records Mean for Your Lot
intro_html:
Broomfield County’s well records need a careful read before you use them to price a home water supply. Colorado DWR lists 1,102 permitted wells, but 52% are classified for monitoring and only 27% for domestic or household use. The 35 ft median depth describes that mixed inventory—not necessarily the well your house will need.

For a property in Broomfield, start with nearby household-well completion reports, then compare the permitted aquifer, depth and tested production.

sections.heading: Why the 35 ft Median Is Not a Household-Well Bid
sections.html:
Depth is reported for 605 Broomfield County wells. The median is 35 ft, and the middle half runs from 20–200 ft. That spread alone makes a countywide average a weak basis for a fixed drilling budget. Monitoring wells dominate the use mix, so the shallow records should not be treated as a residential construction standard.

There is also a substantial deep-well group: 17% are at least 600 ft deep, and the 90th percentile is 880 ft. Permits name Alluvial and Laramie Fox Hills aquifers, while many leave the aquifer unnamed or use a fractured-bedrock category. Your target water-bearing formation and its depth beneath the lot matter more than the county median. Ask for a bid tied to comparable household wells.

sections.heading: Broomfield Yield Reports Leave Room for Caution
sections.html:
Only 76 wells report a pump yield. Their median is 10.0 gpm, with the middle half between 5.0–12.9 gpm. That is useful background, but it is a small slice of the permit inventory and not a promise of household supply.

The low end deserves attention: 13% of reported yields are under 1 gpm. A buyer looking at a well in that range needs a pumping and recovery test, along with an assessment of storage and household demand. A pump’s rated capacity is not the same as the well’s sustained production.

Before closing, compare the original yield report with current performance. Also verify permitted uses; having enough physical water does not automatically authorize irrigation or other outdoor use.

sections.heading: Shallow Water Readings Do Not Establish a Countywide Trend
sections.html:
The 49 reported static water levels have a median depth to water of 11 ft, with the middle half at 10–19 ft. Static level means the water level in a resting well. It is not the drilled depth, the thickness of the water-bearing formation or the level the water will hold during pumping.

These figures do not establish whether Broomfield County’s water table is rising or falling. The supplied records contain no water-level series by decade, and different well types can measure different groundwater conditions.

For a purchase, ask for dated measurements from the actual well and compare resting level, pumping level and recovery. A shallow resting level does not rule out weak production.

sections.heading: Permit Activity and the Names Behind the Records
sections.html:
Broomfield County has 1,102 permits on record, with 508 wells recorded as constructed. A permit count is not a count of operating household wells. Recorded issuance was highest in the listed decades during the 1990s, at 244, followed by 199 in the 2000s. The 2020s contain 136 permits, with the newest permit year listed as 2025.

The most frequent driller-field entry is “Authorized (Pe, Pg)” at 392 records; that label should not be treated as a drilling-company recommendation. Named drillers include Waneka & Son Drilling (Waneka, Don), with 54 records, and High Plains Drilling (Jecminek, Charles L.), with 43.

Use these entries to locate relevant completion reports, not to assume current availability or residential specialization.

sections.heading: What the Broomfield Drilling Estimate Includes
sections.html:
The cost model uses Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock and a drilling rate of $50–$70 per foot. At the county’s 35 ft median depth, that puts the drilled hole at about $1,800–$2,400. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is estimated at $7,800–$14,400.

Those are median-depth model estimates, not a dependable budget for every residential lot. The monitoring-heavy inventory and the deep-well share make that distinction important. A household well targeting a deeper formation needs its own depth assumption and written estimate.

Have the driller identify casing and grout requirements, testing, equipment access and what happens if more drilling is needed. Keep the well quote separate from septic, driveway and house-site work.

sections.heading: Water Quality, Weak Wells and Site Constraints
sections.html:
The environmental map lists 1,390 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 209 historic mine features and 188 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. These are screening records across the surrounding area—not proof that a particular Broomfield County well is contaminated. Sampling locations also do not necessarily indicate confirmed contamination.

Review the nearest mapped records and their actual findings, then arrange appropriate laboratory testing of the property’s water. Include routine drinking-water checks and discuss site-specific contaminants with the laboratory or reviewing agency.

For a new build, check well and septic placement before fixing the house footprint. Ask how the drilling contract handles an unsuccessful hole or inadequate yield, and preserve access for drilling and future well service.

sections.heading: Before Buying a Broomfield Lot on Well Water
sections.html:
Start with the parcel’s DWR permit, not the seller’s description of the well. Confirm authorized uses, construction documentation and whether the existing or proposed supply fits your plans. Household-use restrictions can matter if you expect to water landscaping or keep animals.

For neighboring comparisons, begin with Broomfield records that match the intended use and aquifer. Adams County and Boulder County are each about 13 miles away, but proximity alone does not make their wells valid comparisons.

Make water quality, current production and legal supply part of your purchase review. On vacant land, discuss permit eligibility and any applicable augmentation requirements with DWR before committing to construction. Coordinate the well location with septic, drainage, driveway access and the proposed building area.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Broomfield County?
faq.a: The median recorded depth is 35 ft, and the middle half falls between 20–200 ft. However, 52% of permitted wells are for monitoring, so those figures are not a residential drilling target. With 17% of recorded depths at least 600 ft, buyers should compare nearby household wells in the same aquifer before budgeting.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Broomfield County?
faq.a: The supplied model estimates $50–$70 per foot for Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 35 ft median depth, the hole costs about $1,800–$2,400, or $7,800–$14,400 finished with pump, tank, trenching and electrical. Because monitoring wells heavily influence that median, a new household well needs a site-specific depth estimate and quote.

faq.q: How much water do Broomfield County wells produce?
faq.a: Among the 76 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 10.0 gpm and the middle half is 5.0–12.9 gpm. But 13% report under 1 gpm. Before buying, get a current pumping and recovery test; an old permit yield does not establish what the well can reliably supply today.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Broomfield County?
faq.a: The countywide records cannot establish whether an individual well is safe. The surrounding map includes 1,390 PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles, but proximity is not proof of contamination. Review nearby site findings and obtain laboratory testing of the property’s water before relying on it for drinking.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Broomfield County?
faq.a: The supplied facts do not show a water-table trend. Only 49 wells report static water levels, with a median depth to water of 11 ft and a middle half of 10–19 ft. Those pooled readings cannot establish change over time. Ask for dated measurements and pumping-test results from the well you are considering.
